description: How the atmosphere changed over 4.5 billion years to today's mix.
content_html:
A Planet Transformed

Earth is about 4.5 billion years old. For most of that time, its atmosphere looked nothing like the air we breathe today. Understanding how it changed — and what drove those changes — is one of the most revealing stories in science, because it shows how life and chemistry have shaped each other over geological time.

Key Fact

Today’s atmosphere is approximately 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, and about 1% other gases including argon and a small but significant amount of carbon dioxide. This composition has been roughly stable for around 200 million years.

The Early Atmosphere — A Volcanic World

When Earth first formed, there was no free oxygen in the atmosphere at all. Intense volcanic outgassing during the first billion years or so produced a thick atmosphere made mostly of carbon dioxide (\(CO_2\)), with water vapour, nitrogen, methane and ammonia. This mix is similar to the present-day atmospheres of Venus and Mars — a useful comparison that helps scientists reason about what Earth’s early conditions were like.

As the planet cooled, water vapour condensed and fell as rain, forming the early oceans over hundreds of millions of years. At the same time, much of the carbon dioxide dissolved into those oceans or was locked away into sedimentary rocks and the shells and skeletons of early marine organisms.

Scientists cannot observe the early atmosphere directly — they must reason from indirect evidence. Key sources include: the composition of ancient volcanic gases (which match the pattern of nitrogen, carbon dioxide and water vapour); analysis of chemical signatures in ancient rocks; and comparison with the present-day atmospheres of Mars and Venus, which did not undergo the same biological transformation that Earth did. This is a good example of how scientists build a model from multiple, independent lines of evidence rather than a single direct measurement.

The Rise of Oxygen — A Biological Revolution

The dramatic increase in atmospheric oxygen was driven by photosynthesis. Early photosynthetic organisms — including cyanobacteria and algae — evolved in the oceans and began releasing oxygen as a waste product. Over billions of years, this oxygen accumulated in the atmosphere, gradually replacing the carbon dioxide-rich conditions of the early Earth.

The oxygen increase had two major secondary effects. First, it enabled the evolution of aerobic (oxygen-using) organisms that could release far more energy from food than anaerobic life. Second, high-energy ultraviolet radiation from the Sun converted some oxygen molecules (\(O_2\)) into ozone (\(O_3\)), forming the ozone layer. This layer absorbs much of the Sun’s harmful UV radiation, which allowed life to colonise the land surface.

Key Fact

Carbon dioxide was removed from the early atmosphere by two processes: dissolving in the oceans (and being incorporated into carbonate rocks and shells), and being used up by photosynthetic organisms. The biological route is why CO₂ is now only a tiny fraction of the atmosphere.

Stage 1 — Volcanic outgassing: Eruptions release a mixture of carbon dioxide, water vapour, nitrogen, methane and ammonia. No free oxygen present.

Stage 2 — Ocean formation: As Earth cools, water vapour condenses into rain and seas. Carbon dioxide begins dissolving and is trapped in carbonate rocks.

Stage 3 — Photosynthesis begins: Early life evolves and starts removing \(CO_2\) from the air, releasing \(O_2\). Oxygen levels rise slowly over hundreds of millions of years.

Stage 4 — Ozone layer forms: Rising oxygen allows an ozone layer to develop, shielding the surface from UV radiation. More complex life evolves and colonises land.

Stage 5 — Modern atmosphere established: Roughly 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, ~0.04% carbon dioxide. This balance has been broadly stable for around 200 million years — though human activity is now altering the concentration of carbon dioxide.

Nitrogen — The Quiet Majority

Nitrogen makes up nearly four-fifths of the atmosphere, yet it is relatively unreactive under ordinary conditions. It was released by volcanic activity and also produced as a byproduct of biological nitrogen cycling. Because nitrogen is so stable, it has not been consumed by chemical or biological reactions at anywhere near the rate that carbon dioxide was, so it has accumulated to become the dominant gas in the atmosphere over geological time.

The Ozone Layer — A Shield for Life on Land

One of the most significant consequences of rising oxygen was the formation of the ozone layer. High in the atmosphere, ultraviolet radiation from the Sun converts oxygen molecules into ozone. This layer of ozone then absorbs much of the harmful UV radiation before it reaches the surface. Without the ozone layer, DNA damage from UV radiation would make survival on land extremely difficult. The ozone layer therefore represents a critical threshold in the history of life on Earth — once it was established, the colonisation of land became possible, driving a dramatic expansion in the diversity and complexity of life over hundreds of millions of years.
exam_tip_html: Questions on the atmosphere often ask you to explain a change, not just describe it — so include the cause. For instance, saying “oxygen increased because photosynthesis released it” earns more marks than “oxygen increased over time.” Be careful with ancient atmospheric percentages: the spec does not give specific figures for the early atmosphere, so avoid inventing numbers. Only state the modern composition confidently (approximately 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen). If a question asks about evidence, name the type of evidence (ancient rocks, comparison with other planets) rather than making up specific studies.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The early atmosphere was produced by volcanic outgassing and was dominated by carbon dioxide and water vapour, with no free oxygen.
  • Photosynthesis by early organisms was the main driver of rising oxygen levels; carbon dioxide was also removed by dissolving in the oceans and forming carbonate rocks.
  • Today’s atmosphere (approximately 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, ~0.04% carbon dioxide) has been broadly stable for around 200 million years, and the ozone layer it supports makes complex land life possible.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the main gas in Earth's early atmosphere?
A) Oxygen
B) Nitrogen
C) Carbon dioxide
D) Argon
State what is meant by the term 'volcanic outgassing'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: States that volcanic outgassing is the release of gases from magma/volcanoes (1) and gives examples of gases released such as carbon dioxide, water vapour or nitrogen (1).
Secure: Names volcanic release of gases but gives only one example.
Developing: Vague reference to volcanoes releasing something.
Emerging: No creditworthy content.

practice_questions.text: Describe the process by which oxygen levels in the atmosphere increased over geological time.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: States that early photosynthetic organisms (e.g. algae/cyanobacteria) (1) used carbon dioxide and released oxygen as a byproduct (1) and that this process occurred over billions of years, gradually building up oxygen (1).
Secure: Identifies photosynthesis and oxygen release with some sense of timescale.
Developing: Mentions photosynthesis but explanation incomplete.
Emerging: Simple mention of organisms or oxygen with no mechanism.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which carbon dioxide was removed from the early atmosphere.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: (i) CO₂ dissolved in the oceans (1) and was then locked into carbonate rocks or shells of marine organisms (1). (ii) Photosynthesis by early organisms used CO₂ (1) and produced oxygen instead (1).
Secure: Both processes named with partial development.
Developing: One process described adequately.
Emerging: Vague reference to CO₂ decreasing.

practice_questions.text: A student says: 'Scientists have directly measured the composition of Earth's early atmosphere.' Evaluate this claim and explain how scientists actually obtain evidence about the early atmosphere.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Correctly challenges the claim — the early atmosphere cannot be directly observed (1). Names at least two indirect evidence sources, e.g. ancient rock chemistry (1), composition of present-day volcanic gases (1), comparison with Mars/Venus atmospheres (1). Explains why multiple independent lines of evidence are needed to build confidence in a model (1).
Secure: Challenges claim and names two evidence types.
Developing: Challenges claim and gives one evidence type.
Emerging: Vague challenge with no supporting reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the formation of the ozone layer was significant for the development of life on Earth.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains that rising oxygen levels allowed ozone (⁠⁠O₃) to form from O₂ in the upper atmosphere (1); ozone absorbs harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the Sun (1); without the ozone layer, UV radiation would damage DNA and prevent complex life from surviving on land (1); the ozone layer therefore allowed organisms to move from ocean environments onto land (1); this opened new ecological niches and enabled the evolution of far greater biodiversity (1); links back to the fundamental role of photosynthesis in producing the oxygen that made the ozone layer possible (1).
Secure: Four of the above points with logical connections.
Developing: Two to three points, some logical flow.
Emerging: One point, limited development.

knowledge_checks.q: What was the main gas in Earth's early atmosphere?
Which process was most responsible for the rise in atmospheric oxygen over geological time?
options: Dissolving of carbon dioxide in the oceans

knowledge_checks.q: Today's atmosphere is approximately 78% nitrogen and _____ % oxygen.
The ozone layer formed as _____ levels rose, and it absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation from the Sun.
Match each process to its effect on the early atmosphere:
right: Released CO₂, water vapour and nitrogen
Led to the formation of the oceans

flashcard_questions.q: What was the main gas in Earth's early atmosphere?
flashcard_questions.a: Carbon dioxide, produced by volcanic outgassing.

flashcard_questions.q: What process produced the early atmosphere?
flashcard_questions.a: Volcanic outgassing — gases released from erupting volcanoes.
Water vapour in the early atmosphere condensed as Earth cooled, falling as rain.

flashcard_questions.q: Which type of organism first produced significant quantities of atmospheric oxygen?
flashcard_questions.a: Early photosynthetic organisms such as algae and cyanobacteria.

flashcard_questions.q: Name two ways CO₂ was removed from the early atmosphere.
flashcard_questions.a: Dissolving in the oceans and being used up by photosynthesis.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the approximate percentage of nitrogen in today's atmosphere?
What is the approximate percentage of oxygen in today's atmosphere?
The ozone layer is made of which molecule?
Why is the ozone layer important for life on land?
flashcard_questions.a: It absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation from the Sun.

flashcard_questions.q: For approximately how long has today's atmospheric composition been stable?
Why is nitrogen the most abundant gas in today's atmosphere?
flashcard_questions.a: It is very unreactive, so it has not been consumed by reactions over geological time.

flashcard_questions.q: The early atmosphere of Earth was similar to the present-day atmosphere of which planets?

glossary_terms.definition: A colourless, unreactive gas making up about 78% of the atmosphere, built up gradually through volcanic activity and biological cycling.
A reactive gas essential for aerobic respiration and combustion, making up about 21% of the atmosphere, produced almost entirely by photosynthesis.
The process by which gases dissolved inside molten rock are released at the surface through volcanic eruptions, building up the early atmosphere.
The change of state from gas to liquid, which occurred to water vapour in Earth's early atmosphere as the planet cooled, forming the first oceans.
The process by which organisms use light energy to convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen, responsible for nearly all the oxygen in today's atmosphere.
A layer of ozone (O₃) in the upper atmosphere that absorbs most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet radiation, making complex land life possible.
